title: Histograms, scatter plots and correlation
setup:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("study_log.csv")
explanation: Back to the study log. A histogram (kind="hist") shows how values are spread out: how many scores fall in each range. A scatter plot (kind="scatter", x=..., y=...) puts one dot per row, to see if two columns move together. Correlation puts a number on it, from -1 to 1: near 1 means they rise together, near -1 means one goes down as the other goes up, and near 0 means no clear link. Use df["a"].corr(df["b"]). Careful: correlation doesn't prove that one causes the other!

lines.explain: One dot per study session: minutes across, score up. The dots climb from left to right.

tasks.prompt: Predict first: what's the correlation between minutes studied and score?
hints: In the scatter plot, longer sessions tend to have higher scores.
Rising together means a positive number close to 1.

solution_lines.explain: 0.94: a strong positive link. More study minutes go with higher scores. (It doesn't prove the minutes caused the score.)

tasks.prompt: Fill in the blank to plot minutes against score.
Draw a histogram of the scores.
hints: Pick the score column, then plot with kind="hist".

solution_lines.explain: Bars show how many scores fall in each range. Most are in the 70s and 80s.

tasks.prompt: Print the correlation between minutes and score, rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: df["a"].corr(df["b"]) gives one number. Wrap it in round(..., 2).

tasks.prompt: Show the correlation table for the minutes and score columns, rounded to 2 decimals.
hints: corr() on a table of several columns gives a grid of correlations.

solution_lines.explain: Each column compared with each other one. The diagonal is always 1: a column vs itself.

recap: You just learned histograms (spread), scatter plots (two columns together) and correlation (one number for how they move together), and that correlation isn't causation.
